summary: L-Ornithine L-Aspartate (LOLA) is a salt of two amino acids used to treat hyperammonaemia and hepatic encephalopathy associated with acute and chronic liver disease. Ornithine and aspartate act as substrates that stimulate the urea cycle (ureagenesis in periportal hepatocytes) and glutamine synthesis (in perivenous hepatocytes and skeletal muscle), thereby promoting the metabolism of ammonia to urea and glutamine and lowering blood ammonia levels. It is available as oral granules/sachets and as an intravenous infusion in Europe and India. LOLA is not FDA-approved.
indications: Treatment of hyperammonaemia and hepatic encephalopathy in acute and chronic liver disease
Adjunctive therapy to reduce elevated blood ammonia in cirrhosis
Management of latent (minimal/covert) and overt hepatic encephalopathy

Ensure adequate hydration and correct precipitating factors of encephalopathy (GI bleeding, infection, constipation, electrolyte disturbance)
Monitor neurological status during treatment of acute encephalopathy
moa: L-Ornithine and L-aspartate are intermediates that enhance hepatic ammonia detoxification by two complementary pathways. Ornithine is a substrate and activator of the urea cycle (it stimulates carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and ornithine transcarbamylase) in periportal hepatocytes, increasing conversion of ammonia to urea. Both ornithine-derived glutamate and aspartate serve as substrates for glutamine synthetase in perivenous hepatocytes and in skeletal muscle, fixing ammonia as non-toxic glutamine. The net effect is increased ammonia clearance and lowering of elevated blood ammonia, which improves the neuropsychiatric features of hepatic encephalopathy.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to L-ornithine, L-aspartate, or excipients
Severe renal impairment (serum creatinine above approximately 3 mg/dL) - applies particularly to intravenous use
relative: Significant renal impairment (risk of aspartate/amino-acid accumulation)
Conditions requiring strict fluid/sodium limitation when using high-volume IV infusions
Hereditary fructose intolerance if a formulation contains fructose/sorbitol
monitor: Signs of fluid overload during IV therapy

preg: There are limited data on the use of L-ornithine L-aspartate in pregnancy. It should be used only when clearly necessary and the expected benefit outweighs any potential risk, under specialist supervision.
lact: Limited data are available on use during breastfeeding. Use with caution, weighing the benefit of treating maternal hepatic encephalopathy against potential risk to the infant.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment. Intravenous L-ornithine L-aspartate should be avoided when serum creatinine exceeds about 3 mg/dL because of the risk of accumulation. Monitor renal function and electrolytes; adjust therapy and consider the oral route with monitoring where appropriate.
hepatic: Hepatic disease is the primary setting for use, as L-ornithine L-aspartate is indicated for hyperammonaemia and hepatic encephalopathy in acute and chronic liver disease. No dose reduction is required for hepatic impairment per se; therapy is titrated to ammonia level and clinical encephalopathy response. Correct precipitating factors concurrently.

major: No clinically significant major drug interactions are well established
moderate: Drugs that raise blood ammonia or precipitate encephalopathy (e.g. high-dose diuretics causing hypokalaemia/alkalosis) may oppose its effect
Sedatives and CNS depressants may confound assessment of encephalopathy and worsen mental status
minor: Generally favourable interaction profile; commonly combined with lactulose and rifaximin in encephalopathy management
interactions.food: Oral granules are taken after meals dissolved in liquid; food does not adversely affect efficacy.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol, which aggravates the underlying liver disease and may precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy.
interactions.diagnostics: May lower measured blood ammonia (a treatment goal). At very high infusion rates, transient gastrointestinal symptoms may occur; monitor electrolytes during IV therapy.

serious: Volume overload with high-volume IV infusion in susceptible patients
rare: Pain or irritation at the infusion site
Transient changes in electrolytes with rapid infusion
emergency: Acute fluid overload/pulmonary congestion in patients with cardiac or renal compromise

monitoring: Mental status / hepatic encephalopathy grade and neurological examination
Infusion rate and signs of fluid overload during IV use
Resolution of precipitating factors (infection, GI bleed, constipation)
counsel: This medicine helps lower ammonia in the blood to treat confusion caused by liver disease
Dissolve the granules in a glass of water or juice and take after meals
Mild nausea, vomiting, or stomach upset can occur and usually settle; report if persistent or severe
Avoid alcohol completely, as it harms the liver and can worsen your condition
Continue any other prescribed treatments (such as lactulose) and attend follow-up for ammonia and liver tests
Seek urgent help if confusion, drowsiness, or disorientation worsens
pk: Reductions in blood ammonia observed during/after infusion (within hours)
IV: effect tied to infusion; oral peak amino-acid levels within 1-2 h
Constituent amino acids rapidly metabolised (short plasma half-life)
Sustained with divided oral dosing (three times daily) or continuous infusion
Store below 25-30 C, protected from moisture and light
pearls: Works via two pathways - urea cycle activation (ornithine) and glutamine synthesis (ornithine-derived glutamate and aspartate) - to clear ammonia
Meta-analyses suggest benefit in lowering ammonia and improving both overt and minimal hepatic encephalopathy, often as adjunct to lactulose/rifaximin
Avoid IV use when serum creatinine exceeds about 3 mg/dL because of accumulation risk
Always treat the precipitating cause of encephalopathy (infection, GI bleed, constipation, electrolyte derangement) alongside LOLA
Infuse IV slowly (generally up to ~5 g/hour) to minimise nausea and vomiting
missed: If a dose of the oral granules is missed, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take a double dose. Intravenous dosing is managed by the treating clinical team.
overdose: No specific overdose syndrome is established for L-ornithine L-aspartate. Effects would be expected to be extensions of common adverse reactions, mainly gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting), and, with excessive intravenous volume, fluid overload. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with symptomatic treatment, monitoring of electrolytes, renal function, and acid-base status, and discontinuation or rate reduction of any infusion.
